Another bottle of fiber is not going to save your shots.

Not the magnesium your daughter ordered for you off Amazon for forty-six dollars. Not the prune juice your mama swore by. Not the Smooth Move tea from the health food store in East Point.

Read every word of this. The answer is in here and it is not what your doctor told you.

Marcus passed eighteen months ago — September of '24, sudden heart attack at seventy-one, the morning after our forty-fifth anniversary dinner. He was retired from Aflac, he was a deacon at our church, and he was the only man I ever loved.

I have two grown daughters — Kendra in Tucker, Tracey in Decatur — and three grandchildren who keep me alive. I retired from Atlanta Public Schools in 2022 after thirty-two years as a guidance counselor, the last seventeen at Frederick Douglass High. I am active at Greater Mt. Zion AME Church, where Marcus and I were members for thirty-six years, and where I sit on the Mothers Board with eleven other women who have known me longer than my own daughters have.

In the nine months after Marcus passed, I ate. Not from hunger. From wanting something to do with my hands at seven in the morning when the house was too quiet. I gained fifty-six pounds. The constipation started in week four. By month three I was going every six or seven days, and only after a long fight. By month six the fight had stopped working.

The kind I had never had in sixty-seven years of life. I started carrying breath mints in my pocketbook in a way I had not since I quit smoking in 1989.

He told his mother. Kendra called me that night. She did not say it, but she was afraid.

The two women across the table who noticed pretended they did not. I went out to my car in the church parking lot afterward and cried for ten minutes before I could drive home.

I told my prescriber.

"It happens with these medications, Mrs. Mason. Drink water. Try Miralax. Give it more time."

A prescription bulk-former my gastroenterologist wrote at ninety-four dollars out of pocket. Prune juice. Senna tea. A bottle of Smooth Move from a health-food store in East Point.

I had a basket of all of it in my pantry. Tracey saw it when she came over to drop off the grandbabies on a Sunday afternoon. She asked me what was happening. I told her I was fine.

I still had not gone normally in eight weeks. The sulphur burps were keeping me from communion on First Sundays. And meanwhile, my best friend Patricia was disappearing from the only thing she had ever loved more than us.

Pat went on to study music education at Spelman College from '76 to '80, came back to our church in 1985, and was made music minister in 2003. She has been the music minister at Greater Mt. Zion for twenty-two years.

Our congregation does not have a Sunday service without Pat at that piano. Pat has not had a Sunday morning without our congregation since 1985. Marcus called her the heartbeat of our church right up until the day he passed.

She started Mounjaro® a year before I started Ozempic — same kind of grief story, different husband, hers passed in 2021. She lost fifty-one pounds. By December of '24 she was running again — she had been a sprinter at Spelman, I do not know if I told you that — and she was three months into rehearsals for the church's hundredth anniversary celebration scheduled for October. I thought about the night in August when I had taken three Senna tablets and missed the next morning's Mothers Board breakfast for the first time in nine years.

"Will this work for Pat?"

"It will work for Pat if she will take it. Right now, you. Two capsules with dinner. The magnesium pulls water in gently overnight. The ginger speeds your stomach emptying. Regularity inside three or four days. Sulphur burps usually gone within forty-eight hours. Energy back in the second or third week as the B12 builds up."

Day one, nothing. Day two, nothing. Day three, I went, in my own bathroom, gently, at six fifty AM. No cramping. No straining. Just normal.

Week two, I slept through the night for the first time since March.

Week three, I had energy at three in the afternoon for the first time since the spring.

Week four, I kept the grandbabies on a Tuesday and a Thursday and on Saturday I drove down to Athens for the afternoon to visit Kendra's mother-in-law at her assisted living facility. I did not fall asleep once.

I am still on Ozempic®. Down to one eighty-two. My blood pressure last visit was one twenty-eight over seventy-six. My doctor said it is the best she has seen on me in twenty years.

That was eight weeks ago. Haven't been constipated since. Haven't had a sulphur burp since.

She had been preparing the program for two years. Twelve special selections. A full orchestra brought in from Clark Atlanta. Three guest soloists, including the granddaughter of our founding pastor flown in from Houston. Eight hundred people in the sanctuary. The Bishop of the Sixth Episcopal District. Pat had quit her Mounjaro® in February.

Another bottle of fiber is not going to save your shots.

Not Miralax. Not Metamucil. Not the ninety-four-dollar prescription bulk-former your gastroenterologist called in last Thursday. Not the magnesium your daughter ordered for you off Amazon for forty-six dollars. Not the prune juice your mama swore by. Not the Smooth Move tea from the health food store in East Point.

NONE OF IT IS GOING TO WORK.

I know because I tried all of it for eleven months. And nine weeks ago I had a discontinuation appointment on the calendar for a Friday afternoon at one because I was done — done planning every Sunday morning around whether I could make it through service without leaving the sanctuary, done burping behind my hand at the Mothers Board meeting, done watching my own grandbabies and falling asleep on the couch while they watched cartoons at three in the afternoon.

I was going to walk into my prescriber's office at one o'clock, quit my Ozempic, and accept that I would be back to two hundred and thirty-four pounds within nine months. Maybe sooner. I had done it once before, after Marcus.

I almost let it happen. I was still listening to the same garbage that took my best friend's place at the piano.

I live in Stone Mountain, Georgia — twenty minutes east of Atlanta — in the brick ranch house Marcus and I bought in 1989 with the down payment we saved for six years. Marcus passed eighteen months ago — September of '24, sudden heart attack at seventy-one, the morning after our forty-fifth anniversary dinner. He was retired from Aflac, he was a deacon at our church, and he was the only man I ever loved.

I have two grown daughters — Kendra in Tucker, Tracey in Decatur — and three grandchildren who keep me alive. I retired from Atlanta Public Schools in 2022 after thirty-two years as a guidance counselor, the last seventeen at Frederick Douglass High. I am active at Greater Mt. Zion AME Church, where Marcus and I were members for thirty-six years, and where I sit on the Mothers Board with eleven other women who have known me longer than my own daughters have.

In the nine months after Marcus passed, I ate. Not from hunger. From wanting something to do with my hands at seven in the morning when the house was too quiet. I gained fifty-six pounds. The constipation started in week four. By month three I was going every six or seven days, and only after a long fight. By month six the fight had stopped working.

The sulphur burps started in April. The kind that come up without warning. The kind that came up standing next to Pastor Womack on the receiving line after the eleven o'clock service. The kind I had never had in sixty-seven years of life. I started carrying breath mints in my pocketbook in a way I had not since I quit smoking in 1989.

The fatigue is what would have taken me. I am a sixty-seven-year-old woman with three grandbabies between two daughters who both work outside the home. I am the standing Tuesday and Thursday daycare. By July of last year I was driving to Kendra's house at two in the afternoon and falling asleep on the family-room couch while my eight-year-old grandson Caleb built Legos beside me on the floor. He told his mother. Kendra called me that night. She did not say it, but she was afraid.

And the brain fog. I lost the name of my own granddaughter Aniyah at the Mothers Board meeting in August. Just for fifteen seconds. I covered it. The two women across the table who noticed pretended they did not. I went out to my car in the church parking lot afterward and cried for ten minutes before I could drive home.

I told my prescriber.

"It happens with these medications, Mrs. Mason. Drink water. Try Miralax. Give it more time."

A prescription bulk-former my gastroenterologist wrote at ninety-four dollars out of pocket. Prune juice. Senna tea. A bottle of Smooth Move from a health-food store in East Point.

I still had not gone normally in eight weeks. The sulphur burps were keeping me from communion on First Sundays. And meanwhile, my best friend Patricia was disappearing from the only thing she had ever loved more than us.
